title: Grace was told she was too young for endometriosis. Girls should not have to grow up before their pain is taken seriously.
subtitle: A Yorkshire teenager’s experience exposes the distance between recognising endometriosis as a disease that can begin at puberty and getting young patients the care they need.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 19 September 2026.

Grace was 13 when severe pain began disrupting her periods. By the time the BBC reported her experience on 23 August, the Yorkshire teenager, then 14, had received an endometriosis diagnosis after her family sought a second private opinion. She said doctors had repeatedly ruled out the condition because of her age. [BBC report](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ceqe8exvwwwo).

Her account describes repeated hospital visits and pain requiring morphine. What troubled her was not only the intensity of the symptoms, but the sense that she was not believed. “Even a specialist didn’t believe me,” she told the BBC. [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ceqe8exvwwwo).

Age alone is not a sound reason to dismiss the possibility. The NHS identifies endometriosis as a condition affecting women and girls from the onset of periods through menopause. Its advice is to seek medical help when symptoms disrupt everyday life or persist despite treatment. [NHS guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/).

## The problem is not simply a painful period

Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the womb lining growing elsewhere, causing inflammation and scarring. The World Health Organization estimates that it affects about 10% of women of reproductive age. That is a broad population estimate, not a measure of how many teenage girls have the disease. [WHO fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/endometriosis).

![A medical diagram showing endometriosis lesions, an endometrioma and adhesions around the uterus and ovaries.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/202503_Endometriosis_with_annotation.svg/960px-202503_Endometriosis_with_annotation.svg.png)

Medical illustration created 28 February 2026. Illustration: Femke. CC BY 4.0.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:202503_Endometriosis_with_annotation.svg
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

Symptoms can overlap with other conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome. Investigating alternatives is part of diagnosis; it is not, by itself, evidence of dismissal. But uncertainty should lead to a plan for assessment and review, rather than a conclusion that a young person must simply tolerate disabling pain. [NHS diagnostic information](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/).

There is also an important distinction between beginning treatment and confirming every detail of a diagnosis. WHO says a clinical diagnosis may be based on symptoms and imaging, and surgery is not necessarily required before treatment starts. A girl should not be left with the impression that her pain becomes medically meaningful only once an operation has proved its cause. [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/endometriosis).

Grace’s reported experience is one family’s account, not a clinical audit or a measure of how often teenagers are dismissed. ATHENA has not reviewed her medical records. The BBC report does not identify the clinicians involved or include a case-specific response from them.

## A diagnosis should not depend on a family’s purchasing power

The private consultations in Grace’s story raise an access question: what happens to a child whose family cannot fund another opinion? Her experience cannot establish that private care is generally better; her first private consultation did not produce the diagnosis either. [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ceqe8exvwwwo).

The wider barrier is documented. WHO says access to early diagnosis and effective treatment remains limited in many settings, including low- and middle-income countries. It describes diagnostic delays of four to 12 years. Those figures should not be presented as a specific waiting time for Uganda, Britain or adolescents alone. [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/endometriosis).

For health services, the accountability question is practical: when symptoms continue, who reviews the treatment, who considers referral and who makes sure the patient is not repeatedly returned to the beginning? For schools, support should start with the difficulty a pupil is experiencing, rather than depend entirely on whether she already has a specialist diagnosis.

## Care must protect the life she is living now

Treatment can include pain relief, hormonal medicines and surgery, depending on individual circumstances. Hormonal contraception may be prescribed to manage symptoms; its use does not imply anything about a teenager’s sexual activity. The NHS also recognises the need for support with persistent pain, fatigue and mental health. There is currently no cure, although treatment can help. [NHS treatment guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/).

For families, the useful starting point is a clear account of symptoms and how they affect daily life, shared with a qualified clinician. Persistent or worsening symptoms warrant reassessment. That is not a demand that parents diagnose endometriosis themselves, nor a suggestion that all severe menstrual pain has the same cause.

Grace chose to speak publicly to help other teenagers pursue answers. The responsibility should not stop with girls learning to insist more forcefully. A health service that takes adolescent pain seriously must offer a route from the first complaint to assessment, treatment and follow-up—before missed lessons, friendships and ordinary days become the price of being believed.

*Reporting note: This feature follows up the BBC’s 23 August report; it does not claim a new development in Grace’s treatment. Clinical context comes from NHS and WHO guidance.*
